newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH OUTPUT GRINDS TO HALT AS CBANK MEASURES BITE.
newsitem.headline: CZECH OUTPUT GRINDS TO HALT AS CBANK MEASURES BITE.

text.p: Czech industrial and construction output posted their second consecutive monthly contraction in February, as the central bank's restrictive monetary policy continues to stifle economic growth.

The Czech Statistical Bureau on Wednesday said real industrial production contracted 5.8 percent, year-on-year, in February, while construction output also slumped, shrinking a real 1.6 percent over the same month of the previous year.

It was the second time in as many months both have fallen, and analysts said the figures could be attributed mainly to the central tight monetary policy that has cooled the economy in an attempt to choke inflation.
"The figures are not particularly surprising.It's obviously a result of the tight money policy the central bank has put in place," said Jonathan Garner of Robert Fleming Securities.

"Unfortunately it's painful and it takes time for that to begin to affect wage growth and the trade balance which remain the two main problems but there are signs it is working in terms of M2 money and the inflation rate," he added.

The Czech economy has enjoyed several years of demand-led growth as industry imported technology and the population, which has seen its wages rise sharply over the past few years, slaked its thirst for consumer goods.

Last summer, the central bank hiked its key discount rate by one full percentage point to 10.5 percent, and implemented a series of measures incluing repo rate hikes and raising minimum reserve requirements to choke a burgeoning money supply and ease inflationary pressures.

The moves appear to be working, with the M2 money supply, which measures currency, demand deposits, time and savings deposits, and foreign currency deposits, easing to 7.8 percent in December from 20.2 percent in the same month of 1995.
On Tuesday the CSU said inflation fell to an all-time low of 6.8 percent, year-on-year in March.

In Thursday's report, the CSU said that wage growth slowed in February to a nominal 11.4 percent, down from 14.4 percent the previous month. But analysts said it was too soon to see a real trend in the figures.

"It's starting to affect the real economy but it is going to take time for that to seep through to wage growth," said one local analyst. "Particularly with the low unemployment rate the trade deficit and that is why we are seeing the central bank constantly stating it will not back off higher rates."

The government has said it will introduce a package of measures to help the economy on April 16. Though it has not mentioned specific measures, local media have reported an import surcharge and public sector wage limits as solutions.

Ironically, while most of Europe continues to battle high unemployment, analysts said they were disappointed with data released on Wednesday that showed the jobless rate dropped to 3.9 percent in March from February's 4.1 percent.

"We were a little disappointed with the unemployment figure yesterday which was a little unexpected. But that is the only figure this week that has not been in line with our expectations," said Lubos Kacmarik of Creditanstalt.
"The wage growth figure is good...it comes close to the central bank's magic number of 10 percent," he said.

Analysts said the market is now keenly focused on January M2 money supply figures, which are exepcted to be released on Thursday, which may prove to be the final data that convinces the central bank to move on rates.

A flood of some 35 billion crowns worth of crown- denominated Eurobonds was issued that month and the central bank has been working furiously to keep the funds that came into the Czech Republic in the form of swaps to back the paper out of the money supply.
"There is a threat to M2 in how much of the Eurobond money came into the economy. We will see if the central bank has been successful in sterilising," Kacmarik said.
